newsitem.title: USA: Fed hopefuls unlikely to shift credit policy focus.
newsitem.headline: Fed hopefuls unlikely to shift credit policy focus.

text.p: The expected nomination of two new members to the Federal Reserve Board is unlikely to either influence or change the course of central bank monetary policy in the near term, according to former Fed officials and Wall Street experts.
"I don't think you're likely to see a significant change in the direction of monetary policy," said William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

White House officials over the weekend said President Bill Clinton is expected to name Roger Ferguson, a partner with consulting firm McKinsey & Co Inc, for one of the two vacant spots at the Fed Board.
Clinton also has approved recommendations from members of his staff to name Edward Gramlich, an economist at the University of Michigan, for the second spot on the Board.

Ferguson and Gramlich now will undergo further background checks. No problems have cropped up so far and given the expectation that none will emerge, Clinton may choose to formally nominate the two candidates, U.S. officials said.
The two economists would then have to be confirmed by the U.S. Senate, which must approve the White House appointments.

If Ferguson and Gramlich are approved, Clinton will have nominated five of the seven members of the the current Fed Board, including chairman Alan Greenspan, who was first appointed by President Ronald Reagan, reappointed by President George Bush and reappointed again by Clinton.

While some expressed concern such a composition could make the Board a bit more "dovish", most said the arrival of two new governors would not change the apparent consensus among members that monetary policy must be preemptive.
"The Fed will maintain its position of fine-tuning interest rates in anticipation of inflation," said Ford, who is the Banking Chairholder at Middle Tenessee State University.
Analysts also said the Fed's underlying approach to monetary policy was unlikely to change since neither Ferguson nor Gramlich were perceived to be monetarists.
Monetarism is a theory that advocates strict control of money supply as the major weapon of monetary policy, especially against inflation.
The timing of the possible nominations also was seen as another factor in favor of the maintenance of the Fed's current monetary policy course over the short term.

Analysts said the nomination process usually takes some time, which would likely keep Ferguson and Gramlich out of the next meeting of the Fed's policy-setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), on May 20.

"They're appointees and they probably won't even be confirmed until some time towards the end of the summer," said Michael Strauss, senior vice president and chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
"The idea of these guys voting in May, voting in July, is limited. It might even be August or later before they go through the full approval process," Strauss said.
Also adding to expectations of the status quo at the Fed Board, was the perception that Edward Gramlich is believed to be a reputable consensus builder.
"I've known Ed well. I've known him for years and I've always admired the way he handles issues," said Robert Holland, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.

"He's not cantankerous or insistant on his own point of view...He has his own opinion and he always expresses it very effectively. But he also understands building a consensus in a group," Holland added.
While Gramlich appears to be a known figure in Washington and on Wall Street, analysts said they knew very little about Roger Ferguson and his opinions about monetary policy.

"We don't know much about Ferguson," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "It was a surprise...(but) given that he's a Clinton appointee, you probably should lean toward him being on the dovish side."
Analysts also said it was important to note who the likely candidates were replacing.

The spots on the Fed Board were opened earlier this year with the departure of Janet Yellen for the White House Council of Economic Advisers and Lawrence Lindsey for the conservative American Enterprise Institute think tank.

"Yellen was already a dove, so at least one of the nominations will not change the balance of power in the Board," said a Fed watcher for a major Wall Street investment firm, who asked not to be named.
"So the question is who will take Lindsey's spot, since Lindsey was a Republican appointee and therefore seen as being a more conservative economist," the Fed watcher said.
The current members of the Fed Board are -- Alan Greenspan, Chairman; Alice Rivlin, Vice Chairman; Laurence Meyer, Governor; Susan Phillips, Governor; and Edward Kelley, Governor.
Greenspan, Rivlin and Meyer are Clinton's appointees. Phillips was nominated by Bush in 1991 and Kelley was first nominated by Reagan and then re-appointed by Bush.
The Fed last changed interest rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to its current 5.50 percent target.
